question_text: Two Barangay patrol cars start their rounds from the municipal hall at the same time. Car A completes a round every 12 minutes, and Car B completes a round every 18 minutes. After how many minutes will both cars meet at the municipal hall again?

hint_ladder.title: Identify LCM Requirement
hint_ladder.text: When two recurring events coincide again, find the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of their cycle times.

hint_ladder.title: Find Prime Factors
hint_ladder.text: Prime factors: 12 = 2² × 3, 18 = 2 × 3². The LCM takes the highest power of each prime.

hint_ladder.title: Apply LCM Formula
hint_ladder.text: LCM(A, B) = (A × B) / GCD(A, B). GCD of 12 and 18 is 6.

hint_ladder.title: Calculate LCM
hint_ladder.text: LCM = (12 × 18) / 6 = 216 / 6 = 36 minutes. That's the time both cars meet again.

A.text: Correct! 36 minutes is the LCM of 12 and 18. Both cars will be at the municipal hall after 3 rounds of Car A and 2 rounds of Car B.

B.text: 6 minutes is the GCD of 12 and 18, not the LCM. The student likely confused GCD with LCM.

C.text: 216 minutes is the product of 12 and 18 without dividing by the GCD. The student simply multiplied the two numbers.

D.text: 42 minutes is the sum of 12 and 18 plus 12, a common error of adding the cycle times incorrectly.

next_time_rule: 💡 **Key Takeaway:** Recurring coincidence time = Least Common Multiple (LCM) of individual cycle times. Use prime factorization or the formula (A×B)/GCD.

3. **Compute LCM:** Take the highest power of each prime: 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36.
   Alternatively, use the formula: LCM(12,18) = (12×18)/GCD(12,18). GCD is 6, so LCM = 216/6 = 36.

question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence for a formal administrative order: 'The Regional Director requested that every department chief __ a monthly compliance audit.'

hint_ladder.title: Identify Verbs Demanding Subjunctive Mood
hint_ladder.text: Verbs like 'requested', 'demand', 'recommend', 'require' trigger the subjunctive mood in the that-clause.

hint_ladder.title: Understand Subjunctive Form
hint_ladder.text: The subjunctive mood uses the base form of the verb (no -s, -ed, or modal) regardless of the subject's number or person.

hint_ladder.title: Analyze Subject and Base Form
hint_ladder.text: Even though 'every department chief' is singular third person, the subjunctive requires the base form 'submit', not 'submits'.

hint_ladder.title: Select Correct Base Verb
hint_ladder.text: The correct answer is 'submit' (Option B). The other options violate the subjunctive rule.

A.text: 'submits' is the indicative singular form. After verbs of request, the subjunctive requires the base form 'submit'.

B.text: Correct! 'requested that... submit' follows the subjunctive mood rule: base verb after demand/request verbs.

C.text: 'submitted' is past tense. The subjunctive requires the base form, not a past tense.

D.text: 'would submit' uses a modal auxiliary. The subjunctive does not use modals; it uses the bare base form.

next_time_rule: 💡 **Key Takeaway:** After verbs of request/recommendation/demand (e.g., requested that...), use the base verb (subjunctive). No -s, -ed, or modals.

question_text: Identify the correct usage for official communication (Reported Speech Tense Shift): 'The committee members reviewed the draft, and __ agreed to submit the recommendations before Friday.'

hint_ladder.title: Check Subject Position
hint_ladder.text: The pronoun is performing the action 'agreed', so it must be in the nominative/subjective case.

hint_ladder.title: Select Subject Pronoun
hint_ladder.text: Subjective case for plural third person is 'they'. Objective is 'them', possessive is 'their', reflexive is 'themselves'.

hint_ladder.title: Final Choice
hint_ladder.text: Select Option A ('they'). The other options are incorrect cases.

C.text: 'themselves' is reflexive, used when the subject and object are the same. No reflexive action here.

D.text: 'their' is possessive, indicating ownership. The blank needs a subject pronoun, not a possessive.

next_time_rule: 💡 **Key Takeaway:** Use nominative pronouns (they, he, she, I, we) when performing the action of a verb. Subject position requires subjective case.
